entities.name: Conrad of Piacenza
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Conrad Confalonieri of Piacenza (c. 1290 – February 27, 1351) emerged as a venerated figure within the Catholic Church, transitioning from a prosperous Italian nobleman to a hermit of the Third Order of St. Francis. His life, spanning the early 14th century, exemplified a profound commitment to penance and asceticism, profoundly influencing local religious devotion in Sicily and serving as a model for lay Franciscan spirituality during the late Medieval period. Born into the noble Confalonieri family in Piacenza, Lombardy, Conrad's dramatic conversion narrative underscores themes of justice, redemption, and spiritual transformation that resonated deeply with the societal values and religious fervor of his era.

His transformation began around 1315, following a hunting accident where a brush fire he started inadvertently led to the wrongful condemnation of another man. Overwhelmed by guilt, Conrad publicly confessed his culpability, saving the innocent man from execution but forfeiting his worldly possessions as restitution. This pivotal event prompted him and his wife, Eufrosina, to renounce their secular lives; Eufrosina entered a convent of Poor Clares, while Conrad embraced the ascetic discipline of the Third Order of St. Francis. He initially lived as a solitary near Piacenza for a decade before embarking on a pilgrimage to Rome and eventually settling in Sicily around 1325, where he spent the remaining 36 years of his life in a hermitage in the Val di Noto.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Conrad of Piacenza's life and subsequent veneration solidified a model of lay asceticism and Franciscan spirituality, influencing local Catholic devotion and pilgrimage, particularly in Sicily, for centuries. His story demonstrates the enduring power of personal conversion narratives in shaping religious practice and popular piety during the late Medieval and early modern periods.
